pitfall_counterexample: Witness: families of exactly 2 children, each child's sex an independent fair coin, person drawn uniformly from the population of children. All 4 sex patterns (GG, GB, BG, BB) are equiprobable; enumerating the resulting population of 4 families x 2 children = 8 children gives 4 boys holding 2 brothers in total (only the BB family contributes: 2 boys x 1 brother) and 4 girls holding 2 brothers in total (GB and BG each contribute 1 girl x 1 brother). Hence, in exact rationals, E[#brothers | the person is female] = 2/4 = 1/2 and E[#brothers | the person is male] = 2/4 = 1/2. The difference is exactly 0, so "women have strictly more brothers than men" is FALSE. The same equality is recomputed exhaustively for every deterministic family size n = 1..14 (both sides equal (n-1)/2 exactly) and for all 1820 rational mixtures over family sizes {1,...,5} with weights k_i/12 -- the strict inequality fails in 1820/1820 of them, i.e. in every model in the searched space. Block C reproduces the submission's own 6-child illustration: over the full 64 patterns both averages are 5/2 (equal), while over the submission's restricted 62 patterns (at least one of each sex) they become 80/31 vs 75/31 -- so the asserted strict inequality is manufactured entirely by discarding the all-male and all-female families.
